scenario: AiTA for not trusting a delivery driver? | Today I ordered food off of an app- it's a third party delivery service that picks up the food and delivers your order. Once you pay online, you're given a code that you give to the delivery driver once he gives you your food (I assume that's how the drivers get paid). The app generates a time that you can expect to get your food by, and the drivers are expected to complete the delivery by then, so if you don't get your order by the promised time you often get a percentage of your order cost refunded. Drivers are not limited in how many orders they can pick up simultaneously (they use their discretion to pick up the tickets they want), but if they take too many at once, they will exceed the time limit and most likely suffer a penalty. ​ I had ordered one tea and 2 pastries, for which I only received one. I called the shop and the manager was very apologetic, offering to using the service to send me out the missing pastry ASAP. I had assumed they would just refund me through the app, but that solution was fine too. The shop paid the delivery fee, and I was given the code to give to the driver when my order arrived. About twenty minutes later, the driver called me to ask for the code, stating he was on his way. I thanked him for letting me know he was coming and hung up, to which he called back two minutes later asking for the code again. I replied that I would have it for him the minute he arrived. After another two minutes, he called back again telling me he was nearby and he was running out of time, could he have the code? I told him he would get the code when I got my food. This time I was a bit annoyed, as he knows the rules as a driver and the only way I can guarantee that my food will be delivered is to hold onto the code until my food is here. The guy snapped at me: do you not understand the code is about to expire?! And I retorted back: Well, you better hurry then, right? as nicely as possible before hanging up. I didn't want to argue any longer, but I wasn't about to risk not getting my item by giving up the code. My friend told me that I was being selfish and unkind since the guy might not get paid for the delivery. I argued that since he voluntarily picked up the ticket, he shouldn't have taken ones he couldn't deliver on time. He said something to the effect of, "thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you". ​ So, AItA? Should I have just given him the code and trusted he would still bring me my food? ​ The end of the story is, after I refused to tell him the code, I never heard from him again nor did I see my pastry. The shop manager saw the order wasn't marked as delivered and called to ask what happened, to which I told her the details. She tried to call the delivery guy then, but he had turned off his phone, so she apologized profusely, refunded me through the app, and reported him to the delivery service management. The manager said that he will either be severely disciplined or fired over this.

First, I need to understand the situation properly. The person ordered food via an app. They were missing one pastry. The shop offered to send it via the delivery driver, and they provided a code for the driver to use. The driver called multiple times asking for the code, saying he's on the way and running out of time. The user refused to give the code until the driver arrived with the food. The driver then got angry, and the user didn't get the pastry. The shop refunded them and reported the driver, who might get fired.

The friend says the user was selfish because the driver might not get paid. The user argues that the driver chose to take the order and should manage their time. The key points here are about trust, responsibility, and the rules of the delivery service.

So, the main question is: is it morally acceptable to withhold the code until the delivery is physically present?

Let's break down the responsibilities. The delivery driver's job is to deliver the food. The code is probably a verification method to confirm delivery. If the driver has the code, they can mark the delivery as complete. But if the customer gives the code before receiving the food, the driver could mark it as delivered without actually delivering, which would mean the customer doesn't get their food but the driver still gets paid. That's a risk.

The user's reasoning is that they need to hold the code until they have the food to ensure they actually get it. Otherwise, if they give the code too early, the driver might just take the money and not deliver. That's a valid concern. The driver's behavior of calling multiple times and getting angry might indicate he's trying to get the code quickly to mark it as delivered without actually delivering, which would be bad.

But the friend says the driver might not get paid if the code expires. However, the system probably has a time limit for delivery. If the driver takes too many orders, they might not be able to deliver on time, which is their own fault. The driver shouldn't take more orders than they can handle. So the responsibility is on the driver to manage their time.

The user's action of not giving the code until the food arrives is a protective measure. It's standard practice in many delivery services to verify the delivery before releasing the code. For example, in some apps, you have to confirm receipt of the order, which then releases payment to the driver. If the customer gives the code early, the driver could fake the delivery.

So, the user was right to withhold the code until they see the food. That's a reasonable precaution. The driver's behavior of being pushy and then not delivering suggests he might have intended to not deliver, or was trying to rush to get the code to mark it as delivered without actually delivering. The shop's response (refunding and reporting the driver) supports that the driver was at fault.

Morally, the user's action is acceptable because they were protecting themselves from potential fraud. The driver's responsibility is to deliver the food, and if they can't do it on time, that's their issue. The customer isn't obligated to trust the driver without verification. In fact, it's smart to verify before releasing the code.

So the action is morally acceptable. Therefore, answer 1.
